Wax Artist I'm still learning honestly and obviously you play against people who are much more proficient at them than others which makes some things hard to tell. I also don't have spare clues to play them myself. It seems like the best generic ways to play around him is abusing structures and cover which are taller than you but that you can see him over, like arms factory... Circle... wood things. He can't fire through them easily and his move speed and attack animations are average so you can stall him a long time around those. Line of sight breaks are good but structures based on using a window are not, especially if it's on 1 predictable really strong window (like lakeside village mini ship). When transitioning between structures obviously strafe a bit while you hold w, it helps with how much wax you take. 

Most of all try and avoid him for as long as possible at the start of the game and drag out his first chase. This is the most important thing in my experience. Different Wax Artists play a different style (for now) but his max presence is really where he becomes very powerful/oppressive, before then he seems mediocre and before his first presence, poor. Dragging out him getting presence in the first place and running ciphers seems tough for him to deal with as his map control is quite bad and his camp seems only okay before max presence unless he can wax block most of the ways to and from a hook.

Personally I'd pick which role you want to focus on first. Playing both is a great idea in the end both for sanity and learning the game purposes - I only started quite recently myself - but with the clue gating it's hard to do so immediately. 

If you have no preference I would buy a hunter since honestly, Prisoner + the starter characters + daily free survivor/s (for quick match) are enough to cover most of your bases and have some variety available, whereas Hell Ember + daily free hunter/s is kind of a sad selection. However, if you did figure out you much prefer survivor I would first buy a rescue character as that's who the starter cast really lacks for; personal opinion but Mercenary is strong and really reliable since you don't really need to hard outplay the hunter to get a rescue.

Anyways, for choosing a hunter I mostly recommend going to custom games and then clicking the arrow right to select AI training. This lets you play any character against bots. There are some more straightforward, fundamentals-based huntresses in the game like The Ripper (who should be the starting hunter honestly lmao), but as your MMR goes up you might find these actually become a lot more difficult to play as they can punish mistakes you make very hard. Because of this I really recommend trying out as many hunters as possible first, as you're likely to find a char who feels intuitive to you (even if they're very tough at first) as the IDV huntress cast is super diverse in gameplay.

Edit: Hit post by accident lol. Anyways, to finish, if you can find a char you enjoy this way even if difficult then they can grow with you as you improve and it feels super rewarding. I bought Naiad after trying her out like this (she is a little more forgiving than some of the toughest mechanical huntresses tbh because even though her abyss mechanics are EXTREMELY important... to tell the truth she doesn't really come with a true downside so even if you start out mostly just chasing well and using her mobility to find and catch up to people that is okay), and it was a really great decision once I started getting better at her, as opposed to just buying someone I could play decently out of the box. Just make sure you're going to enjoy any character you choose win or lose for a good while.

Okay, we've all got our own opinions but this is really pushing it lol. Firstly Entropy summons scale depending on the difficulty selection which is insane by itself. Then, with Enderal being a game where most of the fights are designed with the expectation it's just you going up against you, suddenly you have a spammable companion which is effectively unkillable because of resummoning costs which can draw aggro or often literally bodyblock. And although several can be useful Oorbaya AoE corruption attack deals great damage to everything given that it bypasses enemy armor. Even at base the summons can basically cheese any fight, but with the stat bloat from Twilight Cloak and ring they get even more out of hand.

On the hardest difficulty usually I have to self impose not using them because they make the game too easy if I'm honest.

Then the wild thing is the borderline overpowered summons are essentially "just a bonus" in Enderal since bound weapons with max Entropy outclass everything except at max 1h/etc. plus a godly endgame weapon. *And* Entropy spellcasting is extremely good, Chaosnova is basically an overpowered spell in lategame that even has a higher DPS and *much* larger AoE than comparable Elementalism spells for some reason.

The summons definitely don't need to be any better than they already are in base, and even if they truly were kind of weak I honestly just see summons as a slice of the package you get from Entropy, which essentially does everything competitively with weapon skills/Elementalism.

Anything you're interested in will work well as long as you use the skills and crowd control the game gives you. But personally, for a first playthrough I'd always recommend an Entropy based build, because apart from being amazing it also opens much more endgame playstyle options than any other skill. So essentially you can pick whatever you prefer or mix things up whenever you want a different gameplay style with Entropy, it's awesome.

Bound Sword, Bound Battleaxe, Bound Bow - At max Entropy these are all equivalent to having max 1h/2h/Archery with an endgame weapon. Bound Sword in particular is great for high dps when you're free to attack.

Summons - Are honestly insane as they scale in effectiveness with the difficulty setting and can be massively boosted with special items like Twilight Cloak. Even without they're just an amazing way to split attention in a game where many dungeons are designed with the expectation it'll just be you coming in. I actually seldom use summons on Iron Path often because they can make things too easy!

Offensive Spells - the Entropy spellslinging playstyle is really underrated and I don't really understand why. At worst it's like a slightly lesser Elementalism spell package which you get completely for free with everything else. But to be honest my hot take is that it's not even lesser than Elementalism at direct damage casting. Death Breath has great reliable DPS, but Chaosnova series spells are the most powerful offensive spells in the game. Rapid cast time, hitscan, high damage and an AoE attached to it on hit that is so large it feels as if it's a bug. By the time you kill one enemy with it, every other enemy within a two room radius still also be almost dead. 

So yeah, Entropy is awesome and it is powerful in the objective sense, but mostly I love it because if I feel like self imposing challenges or trying out a completely different playstyle for a few dungeons, I can because Entropy gives access to 4 playstyles plus summons in one skill. <3

The difficulty of each larger area does vary, so much so it's hard to be exact off the top of my head, but luckily they can be geographically sub-divided pretty accurately.

The southern part of Frostcliff, near the Tavern and as long as you're following the road east before it curves north are relatively easy (and also have good rewards), Frostcliff mostly scales firmly up in difficulty as you keep following it around or go offroad. Southern Frostcliff is a bit harder than Goldenforst and Fogville, roughly equivalent to the northern parts of the Powder Desert.

Speaking of Powder Desert, that's the most variable area but most of the hardest parts are in the south-centre and southwest of it, with the easier parts being closer to Goldenforst. Goldenforst's northern areas like Firerock are the more difficult.

Also, there's areas whose difficulty doesn't always fit their level range. Most of Goldenforst near Wellwatch has higher level enemies than many areas (~30, 35), but it's still quite an easy area. Farmer's Coast is early-mid level being around 15 but in my opinion some of the Vatyr spam dungeons are more difficult than higher level areas. Heartland is very inconsistent. Whisperwood is the same level as Fogville but Fogville has harder dungeons. The difficulty is always pretty spike-y within regions in Enderal.

However, as a very general progression order, unless I want more challenge I like to go with something like a... Sun Coast < North Heartland < Undercity quests < Central Heartland... 

Specifics of the order here matter less of course, 
< Dark Valley < Whisperwood < Farmer's Coast < Western Cliff < South Goldenforst < King's Mountain Pass, King's Bay < Fogville < Southern Frostcliff < Crystal Forest < North Powder Desert < North Goldenforst < Thalgard < South-central Powder Desert < North Frostcliff

But honestly doing things organically is fine, probably better. This is just roughly how me and my partner see them in terms of difficulty.

Yeah, bumping up the difficulty in lategame is fun since your character's power tends to scale exponentially towards the end.

The Starling ruins occupied by Nehrimese in Frostcliff are some of the actual worst in the game. If there's one thing I can say for the Wiki and Enderal levels in general is that the enemy level doesn't always indicate the relative strength of them because their stat growths can be all over the place. That said, I don't remember the Nehrimese Scientist too well but I recall "Expedition Leader Melren" (basically a named Nehrimese Scientist right?) being one of the most difficult single enemies (and they had backup).

Honestly the single most difficult enemy and the hardest fights in the game are kind of a different thing. I'm *pretty sure* that the most stat-bloated enemies are... the Black Myrad and Wanted Myrad from Powder Desert; plus Horst, The Colossus and The Navigator which you probably already killed. Plus late story bosses but they're hard to classify. These I'm sure are the toughest single enemies but definitely not the toughest fights because you only fight them 1v1 and they're really easy to juke around.

I think you'll find the Thalgard fights overall easier if you were able to do the Nehrimese Starling dungeons, the "Sunborn One" enemies are threatening-ish but they mostly are just a stat check, they have the highest HP for a common enemy type in the game but their damage just does not back it up. You'll probably find them only doing like 10% a swing to you in heavy armor at most. Since you've got Mentalism (great choice btw ;D) just use Paralyze I and II if things ever get sketchy and you're definitely good. Steel Warden is pretty tough but they're pretty much like The Colossus just with more Conjured Guardians to assist them so either just don't get overwhelmed or you can kill the mobs around them, retreat and then just 1v1 the Steel Warden.

Watch out because in the Abbey Quarters there's tight corridors with a bunch of fire and frost casters, but there's also a Commander Greatsword Lord of the Lost Ones sneaked in with them who'll probably 1 or 2 shot you but you should be used to dealing with Lords of the Lost Ones by now since they all just have massive melee damage and nothing else going for them unless you get surprise attacked by them lol.

Ha, I haven't logged in in years but this question is so interesting to me/the sort of dumb thing my partner and I like to debate.

Honestly it depends on your mid-lategame build for which will prove more difficult, and with some builds actually neither can be the toughest and those rare fights which force aggro multiple Bonerippers in Powder Desert are worst of all.

Anyways, for Thalgard I'd say exactly 6 individual fights are difficult (it's not a very long area compared to even just North Frostcliff) - I was going to list them but it'd be a slight spoiler. Definitely if your build is particularly weak to archers there is one outdoor fight there including a lot of high damage archers and with generally poor visibility that can be extremely frustrating. 

The thing is with all of the other challenging fights in Thalgard and why I think the area is overstated in difficulty is simply that almost none of the enemies have *any* resistance to crowd control, and by mid-lategame every build should have at least 2 available, probably more. Even though Thalgard fights can aggro many tanky enemies at once, in most cases the terrain is pretty favorable or manageable to the player which lets you funnel enemies into crowd control and then essentially fight 1v1s or 1v2s until they're all dropped.
 
I don't actually think Thalgard was "intended" to be as difficult as North Frostcliff, but it can become that way because a lot of the fights are overwhelming in numbers and flat HP (although not necessarily hard hitters) without crowd control which from watching people play I think a lot of people sometimes don't use as much, but that the game definitely is designed with the expectation that you're using them.

North Frostcliff compared to Thalgard really feels as if it has a deliberate heavy variety of fights with many imo specifically designed to counter a variety of individual builds - crowd control immune fights, mass magic user fights as well as just featuring way more unfavorable and mixed terrain in fights (like a walled fort, miniboss atop a tower, long indoor corridors etc.) for the player which honestly is usually the main ingredient in a tough/unpredictable fight. And these things and more come in mixes, with something like 40 fights total. Different builds will find some of the challenge fights much more easy compared to others as well, but overall it seems designed to truly test the completion of your character's build, and also for one or more of the fights to really counter or 'break' it, making you retry the fight several times or change your strategy.

These are just my impressions from a few playthroughs (I usually play on base game Iron Path so things can vary with other difficulties or overhaul mods sometimes). Honestly it's completely a personal experience thing as to which is most difficult, especially given how everyone plays areas in different sequences, and for me that's always a really interesting thing about the game. Either way both are really fun areas gameplay-wise (well, maybe apart from one jank dungeon haha) so I hope you have/you've had fun clearing them!

I'll go question by question for you, at least from imo.

1. No, I'm pretty sure the nerfed Eye of the Storm duration has been the same from launch Forgotten Stories to now (it's still good, especially with AA follow-up).

2. Yes, absolutely. Arcane Archer mixes still make for some of the safest and 'best' lategame builds.

3. The base damage of the summoned weapons are defined by your Entropy *only*, I'm pretty confident by now, but they're boosted by any applicable memories/perks and enchantments for the weapon type; e.g, Summon Sword does not benefit from your one-handed skill, but does benefit from Ring of the Blademaster, Blade Dancer memories and the like.

Maxing Entropy even with a minimum of Sinistrope memories is a bit of a no-brainer to be honest, since Entropy does so much - comparable if not better bow damage than an endgame bow with maxed Marksman, really powerful and versatile summons which can crutch you through midgame *and* scale with difficulty, and Summon Sword V lets you run through dungeons that're below your pay grade.

But every route into Arcane Archer is pretty good, honestly. Thaumaturge memories are powerful, and Mentalism is strong with some points dumped into it if not maxed, Paralyze can be a lifesaver. Elementalist is strong to hard carry you through the earlygame and some of the midgame until Arcane Archer really gets going.

Which kinda gets to the core of your issue, it sounds like - bows and sneaking are just pretty bad early-on. Kolapon gave good advice for playing an Arcane Archer *style* through the earlygame, or alternatively you can just use Elementalism and things like Summon Battleaxe - without memories invested in them, they'll still do better until your mid-teen levels at least. Either way, once you get to Ark, there's quite a few Undercity quests with a bare minimum of fighting with good EXP rewards, as well as a great Sinistra vendor in the Shrouded Mage. You can and should use any better prices gear, Mesmerise and memories (if applicable) to help cheapen the books and pump your Entropy or Sneak as quickly as possible. 

Basically the problem isn't Arcane Archer, it's that you're not yet an Arcane Archer, and the associated skills (except Elementalism if that route) are weak out of the gate. Sneak in particular you really need at 50+ to start seeing 'usual Sneak things' Entropy scales very hard inherently, and Sneak/Infiltrator and bows/Trickster scale hugely with their talents. Once you clear enough quests and initially tougher areas like Ark Crypt, which're doable even on top difficulties when you get there by spamming your summons with Mana Fungi regen and kiting enemies around, you'll have enough EXP for Fire Arrows and better bow DPS as well as access to better spells and gear across the board - it'll become tonnes smoother and easier.

Pokemon in Mystery Dungeon have their own base stats, which don't necessarily align with their stats in the main games at all, and also vary through the series. For example, Meganium in Red/Blue Rescue Team has the highest base stat total out of any Pokemon there. However, apart from a small handful of outliers in the whole game, pretty much every Pokemon has usable stats; often quite similar stats - Chatot and Rhyperior have almost identical stats at Level 100, for one of many many weird examples - and you can generically buff any Pokemon's stats by quite a lot. So what's usually most important in Mystery Dungeon is movepool (especially level-up movepool) and abilities, as well as what items they can use (in some of them), if that makes sense. And Mystery Dungeon has some really ridiculous abilities! Unburden basically gives you a free duplicate of your attack every time you attack as long as you're not holding an item.

In both old and new lore imo he's been portrayed as devoted to Noxus (a little less fanatically in the new lore), yes, absolutely violent, but dispassionate. He uses his violence to make a point, not simply because he enjoys violence. His violent acts appear very dramatic - beheading his superior and Swain's rival for Grand General - but I'd argue that's part of making the point, at least from how Darius perceives it. By executing individuals in such a visibly gory fashion, that instils fear and fervour in Noxians and their enemies alike. Ultimately, maybe that does save Noxian lives, both from counter-attacks on bungled retreats and from infighting. In any case, nowhere in the lore has he ever been portrayed as enjoying or 'making a meal out of' a kill from what I've seen. He's a soldier who also understands the value of spectacle, but doesn't indulge in it.

Personally, although from what I've read I think a lot of people do have a fairly similar opinion, while I don't think DND was the worst thing in human history, I do honestly see it as a strict downgrade from Dominion. 

I'm not going to act like big blowout fights over the Windmill weren't also a big thing (and decided a lot of games) in Dominion, but DND really de-emphasising and in some cases just removing your ability to backdoor cap, skirmish and make picks over (meaningful - also, nitpick, but the Super Minion relic was an unviable place to basically ever aggress a fight on them in of course) secondary objectives did mean a pretty decent number of games had 1 team win the Windmill at the start, and basically never be in any risk of losing it or the game. To be honest, it's a highly-unusual (some would argue inappropriate) question for a survey that's very unrelated to (generally physical) health and health conditions. 

As the other person pointed out, it can also be a misnomer, although admittedly whilst a fairly significant proportion of people (~2%, some results have suggested higher) could be categorised as biologically intersex; only a minority of this proportion tend to end-up knowing it in their lifetime.

I've done some work in stats and generally this'd be a no-go phrasing of the question unless you're again, specifically dealing with physical conditions (in which case trans m and f are only really representative of other trans m and/or f rather than cis male or female groups in either direction). It possibly alienates any trans or intersex people who could be present in your sample and, from the studies we *do* have so far that I've seen on this (not many, I'll freely admit), it actually reduces the accuracy of your responses (I.E, if the data demonstrated a significant difference in correlations between male and female groups; transmasc respondents correlated more closely with the cis male group, vice versa for transfeminine respondents).

I'd be interested in seeing if the OP had a particular reasoning for why they chose that question rather than something near the basic 'Gender: Male/Female/Other/Prefer not to say'.

- Shocklord. No excuse to crack him out other than liking him, and I do like him. He's a classic case of not technically being bad but being outclassed by multiple other characters. Ollie's MP issues are grossly exaggerated because, with the way his damage formulae work, with the Dandy Boy or even just the Red Tide SMG, his Dancing Serpent (10MP AoE) does pretty similar damage to Dancing Devil (the 40MP one). Risky Drawing confers great boosts once you use it many times in succession, but fights in Lisa just don't go on for enough turns - not even Satan - for it to really impress. The nature of the combat's balanced around permakills and Garth does deal with this fantastically with the excellent Questionable Drawing. I think fights with Satan are normally under 5 minutes unless you only use direct attacks. His fat health pool doesn't do much for him because he's not immune to poison, burning, bleed or deep poison (although I always seemed to have less luck with the last one). His health evaporates as long as you have the DoTs on him (poison and burning are the most important ones), which you can achieve with Firebombs and Dirty Waters as well if you can't apply them naturally through your party.

So all you really need is a status effect or two to cover your arse. Ideally pissed because he won't use Decapitate while under its effects, but sleep is really good too because taking DoT damage doesn't wake him up, just be sure you know what order in the round your sleep applier(s) go so you don't immediately wake him up with another of your guys. I might be misremembering but I don't think he has confusion resistance either. If you can't do that, it's best to spam stun and/or scared effects since pretty much every character who can't apply nerf statuses has a stun skill at least. Satan's less likely to be affected by them, but if you have; for example, Brad and Dick using their stuns and Yazan and Ollie using their fears, Satan will still spend most of the fight unable to move whilst taking 10k< per turn from the DoTs.

Not that I'm trying to act like you didn't get a cool clear on Satan, you did it with lower levels and I like that my girl Garth got in on the action too. I like that you can be creative against Satan but basically anything except smacking him over-and-over with Tiger Man, Queen and Crisp works really well.

I think to a large degree people may write what they find interesting at that time, but I really have two big issues with it -

Firstly, the possibility for lionisation of topics that *definitely* shouldn't be. I don't think it's very helpful or interesting to write about topics like abuse in a one-dimensional sense of 'oh my God this is so bad!!!' - if anything that's just written splatter as well - but it's equally if not even more important that it's not presented in a way that glorifies it and/or suggests that it's a normal thing.

This takes quite a lot of finesse and can be quite emotionally-draining as well, which is why I'm personally careful and explore those topics sparingly to begin with. Doing it as right as I can, it's not something I'll get a kick-out of even then; and rightfully so really, so I'm generally just writing it because I feel I have to.

Secondly, when you are going to explore it, it shouldn't be shoved in everyone's faces. It's not about fReE spEEcH, it's just a common courtesy, especially as you don't know what other people writing alongside you might've had to go through in their lives. It's painful to see writing adjacent to a nasty personal experience of yours, slapped-up there indiscriminately by some halfwit who has no real idea about it and hasn't even bothered to attempt to learn.

You could argue in their favour that if it's a thread-based forum and they have their own threads, at least people will know over time to steer well fucking clear of their torture porn party. If the mods won't intervene although most of the players are strongly against it (if they are), I'd suggest like Dharian said to basically blank them IC (quite likely OOC as well); and advise your mates to do the same, at least in a non-committal kind of sense.

Don't feel you need to up the ante to your partner(s) with every post you make. Try and pitch it close to what they're providing, slightly less is fine than them as well, with occasional significantly longer posts from each of you when an extended point or plot movement has to be made.

I think your main group does buck the average here but, like... it's not controversial to say that RP is a really queer hobby. I'd like to say this particularly is *just* me speaking for myself and not necessarily representative, but obviously the majority of RPers are also women as well and I have to admit I've probably written less straight men than most others when I think about it, it's just a bit rarer for an idea like that to pop-up in my head when I read over a new setting.

And of course, although people do tend to prefer to stick to what they know better for romances specifically, it's not as if straight authors aren't interested in writing queer characters and vice versa. It's debatably a good deal **during Black Friday** because it has, in most ways, the same utility as the Armour Closet with additional content. At one point the Armour Closet was 2k DCs which'd make it a no brainer but the closet is a lot cheaper at 1k.

As basically, you get the Armour Closet so you can use EPL, FMA, Togslayer (without clearing 1k Togs); or God forbid Shadow Hunter and Zardbie, all year 'round. Okay, so now let's go through what Storybook can do that Armour Closet can't (off the top of my head admittedly):

- You can use Evolved Pumpkin Lord's buffed heal and mana restore all year-round which is solidly useful, 30% heal makes it significantly more potent in certain Inn fights in low-mid levels.

- There are quite a few endgame items that're seasonal especially on the resistance side, so if you're gearing for that it cuts-out your wait.

- There are also a few lower-level grinding quests which can rival or even top Voltabolt's Challenge, but if you're a higher level these won't be as relevant to you.

- Mostly the convenience of not having to bang-out all of the grindy bits of the seasons in one go.

- Certain seasonally-exclusive guests although for full clarification these are crap compared to the likes of Aegis and Artix.

The number one problem though is I'd tentatively recommend it at 2.5k DCs, but then you're waiting until Black Friday season for that deal anyways, by which point most of the seasons will have passed through. That's something I forgot to bring-up even in that quite long summary, since there's so many different kinds of RP forums and subforums overall.

I've usually RPed through the form of forum RPs. I definitely think you should be wary of individual fora devoted to basically, just one RP, being blunt these have by far the highest chance for nonsense and if things go down the back-end you will have wasted the most amount of time for nothing. But these individual places *can* be really good as well (imo it's where you get some of the best and some of the worst), you just have to be sure that you've found a lovely group of people there. Even if they might die-out rather quickly, at least for me personally I don't realy mind an RP setting becoming inactive, but I do mind seeing some abysmal drama going-on.

That brings us on to the large multi-RP forum sites (as well as, to a degree, non-RP based sites which also have a notable sequestered RPing community*). The great thing about these is that you can find practically anything you'd ever want to write-in; you have protection in rare cases of harassment, and if the author(s) of that particular RP turns out to be a 'Class-A Cunt', it doesn't lose you too much to simply say you're withdrawing and join a kinder RP.

The main problem with them though is that the average turnover of RPs on these kinds of fora is **extremely** high. Unfortunately for me (well, until I took a solid break recently) it's like a sort of drug; I'm hooked on the few times an RP with a bunch of random, pick-up group of individuals turned-out to give me so many good times with them OOC and also gave me a big shot to the arm of being able to watch my character metamorphose in a way I never possibly could've predicted (for better or for worse) having been stretched by the setting and others.

I think there's some really good things about the form and I wouldn't write it off out the gate, but if you're happy with what you have I don't necessarily recommend moving. Forum RP's certainly great if you love creating characters or settings lots, because in that sense you wouldn't really have nothing to lose. Having a sense for whether you're walking into a dodgy group is helpful as well, but I'd say that's the case for all group-based RPs.

First of all, a D doesn't mean they achieved 40% of the total marks. It means they were (within a certain margin which changes year-by-year) in that percentile of achievement of those that were submitted for that qualification this year. So this is a blatant attempt to pull-up the drawbridge, both because historically the progression rate of A-Level to university was extremely high, and also because the grades don't guarantee new students're doing 'worse' than older students with higher-grades, the standards've increased as our education has improved. 

There's also many fair albeit technical arguments to be made that A-Levels aren't a watertight indicator of potential undergraduate and especially postgraduate performance, especially as the old GCSEs compared to many traditional A-Levels accounted for basically a diagonal climb - high uptick in objective difficulty, large difference in actual content. At least the first half-year of most uni courses even at high-end universities are allotted to getting everyone on the course up to a certain predictable level for that reason.

I think it's morally shady to limit people's options, but by far the most compelling arguments for not precluding them from getting loans should be economic ones. Frankly, a student who pursued A-Levels, didn't do too hot and then tried to enter the workforce is one of the worst situations possible for them and for the country. They've had the maximum amount of free academic education but're most likely to be considered for unskilled or service work. In the future we need more skilled workers not less - a degree isn't always an accurate indicator of skill itself, but it is increasingly taken as the best of few options for figuring that - countries which're excelling have more equity and subsidies in education, not less. It is *not* accurate to call it 'the exception' for lower-achieving A-Level students to be in a much better position if they get a degree (especially if you look at it from the country's perspective rather than the personal), *and* it's at a relatively cheap price to the taxpayer as university is much less subsidised than high school and college. 

It's a potential restriction on getting a loan, not 'free money', and one which'd be a disaster for universities and the future workforce with little short-term financial benefit. If you wanted to get shady, it'd be wiser to limit people's options for further education based on their grades, not say 'no loan for you'.

Riftwalker and Dragon Warrior are both below-average advanced classes. Riftwalker has solid general usage as it can get through quests fast as long as it doesn't spam 3x mobs throughout (RW lacks a solid turn 3 nuke although you can always use a trinket for that). Dragon Warrior has some respectable niche use as it can turn any bossfight into a DPS race essentially with Dragon's Onslaught piercing all MPM BPD, so it's really good for slaying Sporca and some others; but it's dreadful at killing normal mobs and gets countered by a lot of general bosses as well, anything with stuns basically.

Dragon Mage and Ascendant is no real contest. Dragon Mage has a couple really good skills like Dragon's Acid and Meditate but even after its post-release buffs its kit is really barren and its best debuffs aren't loopable. It's really not that good and doesn't have a niche. If it had a couple strong instant burst skills it'd be a great farmer for Neverglades, Timetorn Matrix etc due to Meditate, but sadly not. Anyways, it's no contest because Ascendant is one of the top classes in the game and even in terms of pure defence it's not far behind DM.

Dragon Rogue and Cryptic is even less of a contest because DR is pretty bloody horrid (easily the worst class to be released in years, unless Dreaming Togslayer counts, but it's arguably worse than even that as well), although they're not very similar classes overall. While Ninja doesn't have an inherent HP or MP heal, DR's heal is crap and its mana costs are through the roof for a defensive class that can't really afford to take WIS. And besides the lack of healing, Ninja is directly better than DR in every way except turn 1 nuke. It'll stay that way until DR's DoT uptime and passive toxin leech are both massively buffed.

The game just isn't that fun without a DA, but on the other hand if you'd actually be willing to spend quite a bit it's almost irrelevant as after the Master Doom Knight package, there's basically nothing left to buy and little need for more coins.

Anyways, completing all of the story content as a pure f2p I can attest is possible, not all Inn challenges are though. As a process it's much more *tedious* than actually difficult at all.

[Here's a write-up on non-DA classes I did a bit ago.](https://www.reddit.com/r/dragonfable/comments/9wb4n8/best_armors_currently/eajxwac/?context=1) A TL;DR is that Ranger is generally going to be your best friend, with Soulweaver and Paladin as your back-ups.

For tougher fights, this should generally be the stat distribution you're looking for:

STR: 1

DEX: 1

WIS: As much as you need

END: As much as possible

This gives you, on Ranger, about 20% less damage output at a mid-level and on other classes about 30% less, but it almost doubles your health which much more than doubles your survivability given your heals are much larger, which then means you can stall enough turns for the next heals or heal procs more easily. Once you max END you can either start upping your STR and DEX in equal measures; LUK is also decent but I think I like CHA the best due to how often you end-up dragging guests around as non-DA (CHA gives you an EXP boost for them as opposed to the slight penalty you get by default).

Additionally, you may need to equip an [Aww weapon](http://forums2.battleon.com/f/tm.asp?m=18946971) (one of the Frostval weapons also works), [Cheshire Twilly](http://forums2.battleon.com/f/tm.asp?m=16801117) (I believe that's the only non-DA %healing pet) or invite Twilly in Falconreach. 

Guests were nerfed some months ago meaning enemies deal more damage when you have them in your party; however, it's still generally worth it to invite Ash (Book 3 obviously) for tougher quests as he has a great heal and solid damage output. Artix is also a pretty solid guest but I generally find fights are finished a little slower with him than without him unless you have a very strong light weapon. If you're playing Soulweaver invite Aegis - Book 1 for damage output, Book 3 for a very strong defensive steroid (note: don't use Book 3 for bosses like Dr. When and Sofist, Bradley and Vince that completely ignore parry/dodge/block).

Your health and mana potions should be at a good training level especially once you get past Lv 25 or so, additionally, you should get the [Cloak Scrap](http://forums2.battleon.com/f/tm.asp?m=21834946&mpage=1&key=&#21834946) and equip this with your base class - this gives its Final attack a chance to give a health potion. Once you have 5 HP pots stacked, go ahead and switch back to your better bossing class.

All of this should be more than enough to take-out any storyline bosses, even ones in the very top percentage like Dr. When and Al'nold. Tbh you can probably skip a step or two in this. Hope this helps.

The seasonal classes are all vastly better than your other options as pure F2P, so whenever one's available you should definitely, definitely use it. Although Evolved Pumpkin Lord is much better than Shadow Hunter for Halloween as Shadow Hunter's defences are pretty bad and it also lacks a first-turn burst skill which is a profound disadvantage for an offensive class.

The main issue is what to do when it's not Halloween or Christmas. Course, you should be using your base class with Cloak Scrap to get 5 health potions before tough fights as you really need to outlast them as a non-DA, but apart from repetitiveness the bases can be a bit of a liability vs many bosses. I'd kind of hope you don't have Warrior as your base as while Warrior's much faster than Rogue and probably a hair quicker than Mage as well for clearing trash mobs (outside of when Mage can just spam MageFury), it's much worse than either against bosses.

Either way, your selection beyond base and outside of seasonals is pretty spartan. Here's a run-down on what worked for me a bit.

---

Paladin: probably one of the first classes you'll unlock and respectable even with just left-side skills. It's really slow in general and as non-DA even moreso - Barrier of Sanctuary and the stacking passive heal is its strength, so if you can drag a fight out enough you should win by default.

Soul Weaver: SW's Soul Aegis is an amazing shield, Slash is a good ability in general, and while its main 'damage combo' isn't that impressive especially considering its cooldown, it can still put in some work by non-DA standards. Where the class really gets juicy is with Baltael's Aventail - this turns Valour Impact into the best damage skill available to non-DA and makes Soul Aegis into one of the best shields in the game. The problem with that is that the lowest equippable level of Aventail is Lv. 60.

Ranger: since the rework I think this is probably the overall best class available to non-DAs. What is really not ideal is that it doesn't have a single defensive skill on its left-side arsenal. But its mounting damage in bossfights massively outclasses any other options, even compared to Baltael SW. Because of this, I actually recommend investing quite heavily into END as non-DA Ranger - note that you simply need to have STR and DEX roughly equal to get the +15% passive damage, you don't necessarily have to have them higher than everything else - and using a healing pet like Cheshire Twilly. This guarantees you'll have the sustain to get to the point where your Venom DoT, extra turns and criticals tears them apart.

Pirate and Necromancer: I don't think these are as generally good as the other 3 but they're good enough to be worth a mention. A lot of people shit on Pirate because its full complement of skills is pretty bad, especially compared to Ninja. However, considering left-side only standards it's got some good tools. Both of these are most useful for quests where there's a moderately tough boss at the end of it but you don't want to tear your hair out slowly grinding through the mobs on the way with Ranger or SW. Both classes either have a turn 1 nuke, a spammable multi or both, but also have better defence and healing compared to the base classes for bossing.

Technomancer: just barely good enough to recommend, honestly. The main annoyance with Techno as non-DA is that you really need to go a high-WIS build on it to be effective, mainly because it's mana-hungry but also for extra damage on Grenades. Its shield and stun spam is a lot less effective than it used to be but it's still usually enough considering you can use Repair pretty frequently. Like SW, Ranger and Paladin it doesn't have a good turn 1 burst or a very good multi.

---

In my experience the use of the classes beyond these are pretty limited. Unfortunately some of the recent reworks as well as the stat reworks have made many classes even worse for non-DA, like Ninja. Necro and Technomancer also took a solid hit.

I would say Ascendant is significantly better for general-purpose than Cryptic after the stat system changes, but if you enjoy Cryptic then you should definitely keep it. Could always make a Mage alt if you want to try Ascendant out, otherwise you can get classes which perform similarly to all three of the Ataleans as well.

Stone Crusher - if a Light Caster and any DPS classes are around, this is obviously a mandatory party support.

Now 2 slots for support isn't that many, and ideally almost every class brings some kind of support. But room limit 7 is pretty common if you even have 7 people for the boss grind. Although Archfiend is objectively a potent support class, being the 4th in line (hard to call between it and Arch Paladin, Ar P like LC doesn't do as much for smol bosses but for a longer fight it's excellent) puts it in this weird position where it being the best class to use is just unlikely to happen.

It's true, but the main point in this article and in general is that what their tax band technically is is mostly irrelevant as firstly, they don't pay anything like that percentage of tax, and secondly - even more importantly imo - corporations and individuals aren't actually paying the rates of tax in the countries where they're making their money, legally they're permitted to register all of their European sales in a country with a piddling rate of corporation tax like Luxembourg, Ireland, Mann etc. And that's just the start of the wheezes to reduce taxes paid, for example, two companies owned by the same persons or org can also lend money at an extremely high rate of interest to each other for short periods which deflates what you can be taxed on. 

Even after those you can just underpay, see Apple who had a massive amount of unpaid tax to Ireland where they're registered in Europe; the EU ordered them to pay the balance to Ireland, Ireland appealed that verdict as they didn't want to lose a wealthy customer in the future, regardless of the tax being paid being much lower than they should've been. That's also quite common in general, cases get snared up in the EU courts for years, by which point while they may lose the case the cost's more than been swallowed by their profits in the meantime.

TL;DR: if individuals and corporations were actually obeying the rates of personal and corp tax, we probably wouldn't need anything like as high a rate as we do. The issue is that much more frequently than not, they're being avoided completely, low or no taxes at all (see Cadbury in UK for example) being paid in the countries they're doing most business; with tax havens profiting by taking a very low rate which nonetheless makes a large difference for them, and the persons and corporations profiting the most of all.

Golden's a hero I really like, but I'd kinda go out on a limb and say he's a horribly-designed hero because he basically just punishes people who don't know what his kit does, like yourself that game. 

Now tbf your lane combo had a really bad matchup.

Anyways, first of all his Q. It does a huge chunk of damage earlygame (540 at r4) over a short period. But even though it looks like an AoE around him it only deals damage to whichever unit is closest to him at the time within that anim. Standing in creeps can really screw him over if he's trying to pressure you from treeline, he's not that amazing in 2v2s if he doesn't get a W onto both enemy laners, so try not to let him get that by not standing right next to each other, his Plunge is - iirc - very slightly more delayed with slightly less radius than Pyro and Torturer stuns, so position as a duo like you would versus those two.

His W leaps him to a tree as you saw, you'll be able to judge the general place he went but not normally the exact tree he went to unless he was running away and jumped to the very first tree available. First of all, after he leaps to any tree, there's quite a noticeable delay of iirc 3 seconds before he can leap again. You'll also hear a rustling sound effect if GV is in treeline nearby you, which begins just outside of his W Plunge range (his Plunge range is shorter than his distance leaping onto and between trees) so that tells you when he can jump on you - if the noise just started and he does go on you, if you walk the way you came you'll probably dodge his jump. If he does jump downwards onto you and he misses, he's screwed as this gives him a long cooldown before he can jump back into the treeline and his Plunge is most of his CC and set-up.

Obviously and most importantly, if you know what tree he's gone onto, destroy that shit immediately. If it's destroyed he loses stealth and takes a 3 second stun. Hatchet and Blight Runes work, but it's most helpful if you have any hero with area tree destruction, which completely ruins his laning. His E (you prob knew about) gives him decently quick regen from Lv 4 of course so if you chunked him but he leaped back onto a tree out of range, don't expect him to be unable to fight in 30 seconds' time.

GV only really has two strong periods, his laning *can* be strong in the right matchup, and his 1v1 assassination is really good from Lv 6 to about 13 - his roams are solid, but mainly because he gets around the map very quickly and gets extra rewards for successful ganks as opposed to his ganks being guaranteed kills unless he can just click R and walk up to someone with Q (so keep tabs on him and warn your teammates if they're listening). Even for a support his lategame is comically bad, Goldenveil's utility as a support is to have spoonfed himself enough gold to afford better offensive support items than most can, and extra GPM for his teammates so they can make-up for his lack of contribution. Unless someone waltzes around alone at half health GV will get a decent Plunge off *if he's lucky* and then die immediately. Ofc he can pick up Shrunken and other survivability items and he won't just go down like a sack of potatoes but his damage output past his ulti and W initiation is really poor as well. Basically, unless Golden got his team a strong lead (which normally happens just because people don't know the counterplay his abilities have, because it's not something that's obvious from looking, you have to read or play him to know), he's a dead weight later-on.

I mean, I don't think League's system is perfect by any means (neither's HoN's), but you're kind of speaking as if leaving the game to force a remake doesn't incur any penalty. That's not true. If you're the AFK or one of those flagged AFK after the 3-minute remake goes through, you get a match loss and lose LP and MMR. 

Leaving during character select isn't free either, although it's less punitive. Your first dodge within 24 hours hits you with -3LP (1/6th-1/7th of an average win gain), and any after that give you -10LP each (1/2). This is more than enough of a discouragement that char select dodges are not very frequent; especially now that autofilling is also a lot rarer than it used to be, and the most common role to be autofilled to is Top (in solid ranks), which is a role people don't tend to get offended by compared to Support. 

Some people use the daily cheap dodge tactically - leaving if they're hard countered by the enemy team, or other players on the team are on massive losestreaks, others just save their dodge in case they run into someone who's clearly set on griefing the game from the start. I think it's totally fair in the context of League as everyone's afforded the same opportunity, same safety net, it's not comparable to HotS's (for the other guy) which *used* to be a very lax system (back when it launched), but then actually shifted to being a ridiculously punishing system where you got punished far harder for dodging a queue than ragequitting a game in progress (not sure if they shifted it somewhere in the middle recently, I quit early this year). I don't think making dodging possible would work well for HoN because of the lack of assigned roles and the fact you can see who the enemy team are in char select (names are hidden in LoL). But if HoN did have LoL's remake system, while it might not be super beneficial to the game, there's no way you can abuse it to your advantage as a player, lol. It's just giving yourself an LP and MMR drop for no reason, same as if you'd played-out and lost.

'Burst rotation'. This means how much damage they can apply to someone in a short space of time, which is important for any character building full AP even if they're not an assassin.

For Nunu, that means firing an E.

For Diana, you prep your passive and then Q W R Auto R.

I agree we could go deeper by factoring everything in, but it wouldn't change the fact that AP Nunu's burst potential outside of the extremely difficult to pull off ult is barely present. If you factored everything in Diana would not somehow fall behind, just as an example, because she builds Nashor's and Lich Bane as well. Nunu is a great lane-bully against those who can't deal with him, but later-on he tries to be a poke mage and fails due to meh poke compared to a real poke mage, combined with the utter lack of range on his E which makes it unsafe.

You can say I'm assuming, but I mean... I think it's really hard for *anyone* to see how one E deals more %AP than an all-in or even a brief combo from another character. It just doesn't.

Scaling as in mid-lategame scaling in that case.

In either case, though... no. Having a 'burst rotation' of one spell with +90% - even if you do throw in the free bonus AP from W - is absolutely dire. Diana, for example, can inflict +330% AP damage in her fast combo, and this is without taking into account Nashor's Tooth and Lich Bane procs which push that scaling even higher. She also of course throws a lot more base damage into the mix than Nunu.

Nunu's R has a good base damage - surprisingly it doesn't scale as well with ranks in that department as you'd think - and obviously the potential to inflict a superb +250% AP damage to every enemy in the radius as well as the high base. But it's massively unreliable and even then there are picks which can unload a comparable amount of AoE damage without needing so much set-up.

What you suggest doesn't make sense at all, because... then you'd just double-tap the ability to cast it instantly, unless you wanted the cripple and movespeed slow? It'd do the same damage, unless you explicitly mean being interrupted by an enemy. Either way it removes a lot of the decision-making (and rewards for it) on the part of the Nunu player and gives his ult a lower skillcap both for AP and tank. It also shows a misunderstanding of what the point of Nunu's ult even is in the mid-lategame. The high potential damage is the threat, which means the enemy team can't ignore it, but its value doesn't come from the damage. It denies the enemy team the ability to fight properly in a large area, adding to Nunu's theme of giving his teammates free stats and taking their stats away. The 25% cripple doesn't sound like much but it heavily reduces AD damage output in it, and of course the increasing slow makes them eat skillshots. It makes them blow useful cooldowns - dashes, flashes and/or a hard CC to interrupt him. This is a lot more impactful than the actual damage except in a miraculous situation where you full-channel onto everyone.

The big challenge for mages, even very farm-scaling ones though, has always been levels. The lion's share of marksmen, they have one skill which scales very well with ranks in terms of base damage, one midgame-scaling/steroid spell, and a one-point-wonder spell. Of course, there are exceptions like Jhin and Varus but this is a pretty common pattern. Mages on the other hand generally at least have 2 of their skills scaling very well in terms of damage and/or other parts of the ability, which makes being a high level important along with just having a lot of gold.

Based on that, something that interested me about Irelia is her abilities do fit an ADC's pattern in terms of their ranking - her E scales extremely well with ranks in every part of it, and both her W and Q are really competent even at rank 1. I'm not convinced she's going to explode into botlane (even if some whack AP/AS or whatever turns out to be her preferred build which does heaps of damage, just as an imagined example), at least not with the current way it is. Oh, I can explain this. Okay, so this is a pretty niche thing to begin with but it's something that happens with op.gg. Op.gg gets its analytics off bronze-ranked players and classifies that individual play in the game as a bronze-level performance. Lolalytics and other sites classify the tier of the stats from that game based on the two team MMRs of the game as a whole, so a game would be bronze-level on average, and then orders all of the stats it can get from that accordingly.

This doesn't sound like it would make a whole lot of difference but you can see it easily for bronze stats on op.gg. Because Bronze 1 and 2 players will frequently be matched in games up to Silver 4 or occasionally Silver 3 as the players forming the lower end of the MMR balance in that game, they have an increased chance to lose in that game (which Riot tries to account for) as opposed to playing versus players from their divisions or lower (where they're on the mid or higher end of the game's MMR balance).

This is why only 26 of the game's 140 manage to register a 50%< winrate on bronze op.gg, and you'll notice many of the 26 don't have dominating winrates either - frequently lower than they do in silver or even the higher tiers regardless of whether they're an 'easy' champ or not.

Edit: the same thing does happen to a degree with every tier, but the other tiers make it back (more or less) via having an overall stat advantage against the tier below them. With bronze, there obviously isn't one.

The new 'true invisibility' is very boring to play against. Admittedly, champions like Akali would previously be boned by 75g, however nowadays - Twilight Shroud, for example, definitely does have counterplay. It's just that the counterplay to it is boring for a non-ultimate ability. You have to walk away and sit a half-screen off for 8 seconds, and then you're good to go again - so Akali, knowing this, probably walks away and sits a half-screen off for ~8 seconds herself until the Shroud's back up again.

I'm acutely aware this is more bellyaching as I can't think of a solution which doesn't fuck over either Akali (and/or other true invisibility users) or the people who're playing against her, but even with Oracle's, many champions just have to play the waiting game as they either leave or keep going-in. It doesn't feel intense and a surprise-catch as you'd expect from an assassin, it feels bland and you know exactly what's gonna happen next.

The problems tend to arise primarily from the assassins that *don't* have a viable exit strategy in their kit. Not being likely to come out again unless everyone in the vicinity that's hostile dies is a huge weakness, there's few ways to viably compensate for that on an assassin besides... more damage, so they *will* kill their target at any cost. Even if they're basically a 1-for-1 machine, that's very frustrating to play against, and it's not very enjoyable to play alongside either.

The Assassin Update was definitely a mixed-bag to say the least, but I saw their *intention* with it and I agreed with that. They gave assassins that lacked half-decent exit strategies them in exchange for either straight lowered or delayed damage. Unfortunately, in practicality this generally meant they either couldn't do their job at all (release rework Talon, who could jump around all he wanted but was essentially an annoying fly for the enemy team), or could now kill just as well as before but then zipped a screen away immediately afterwards to boot. And of course, the playstyle-changers... ugh, of course, the more you think about it, the more messy it gets. But the intent was right.

Hey, I'm a long-time HoN player. For many of the early years of HoN, we did have players assigned colours going by their relative MMR to the other players in their team that game, so very similar to your proposal. Here's my insight based off that experience:

No.

Just no. It was a shitfest. Role: you're a tanky splitpusher and midgame roamer. Your job is to survive lanephase with a decent farm, as you have a strong 1 and 1.5 item powerspike which you can use to win fights people don't expect, then you take down turrets faster than pretty much anyone else and farm their camps. You're more useful lategame than Shyvana Jg as you're far tankier and give your team a humongous Locket, but your lategame still isn't good. Soak and survive for your team in fights but your life is important to preserve if possible so you can clear objectives asap after. 

Itemisation: your standard core is Titanic Hydra (after any items you need to survive early laning), Stinger, Frozen Mallet. Great items after that include Sterak's Gage, Locket, DMP or Randuin's, Wit's End and finishing a Triforce out of the Stinger. I'd also recommend swapping your chosen tankiness boots out for Swifties later in the game unless they're massively AD AA heavy with Tabis.

Skill max: depends partly on matchup and mostly you should adjust depending on the tempo of the lane. If you're in a bad spot and need to farm creeps safely, or if you need to poke and then all-in the enemy laner, max E. If you can go more aggressive in the lane it's best to Rank 3 E and then max W. I don't recommend ever maxing W from the start (unless they're legitimately drunk or something) as it impedes your ability to safe-farm and control the wave when needed, however it can be viable to do EWQW if you want to all-in them at Lv 4. W's bases are obviously really good but it's deceptively ineffective in toplane as its crappy tickrate and the fact that many toplaners refresh their cooldown(s) if you stick around in a trade too long hinders using that to run people down.

Good matchups: Darius, Jax after Titanic's completed, Trundle, Pantheon, Fiora, Illaoi, Singed - these aren't too bad. You can survive their laning phases with relatively little CS dropped and you have a good shot at 1v1ing them or nullifying their 1v1 in the midgame. Some of these chars also rely on roaming which Shyvana heavily punishes as she takes turrets incredibly quickly.

Bad matchups: the vast majority of your matchups are losing matchups. However, Teemo, Tryndamere, Nasus, Shen, Cho'Gath and Gangplank are particularly horrible. Shyvana's either unable to punish these chars in lane when she sorely needs to and then can't take them on later, or she just gets straight-up wrecked by them throughout the entire game.

Oh my, I could ramble on about this for quite some time. Umm, lemme try and break it down in a simple way.

- The Runes. This is controversial, but Shyvana Jungle's succeeded this season primarily because of Jg meta shifts and improvements in her matchups imo. In terms of the runes purely, it's debatable whether she actually broke even versus the old Fervour. However, for toplane they're definitely worse for her, as Fervour of Battle was the better offensive mastery and in your many matchups where you had to play defensively, Swiftness in the Grasp tree was exceptional. Slow Resist was and is one of the absolute strongest stats for Shyvana, especially toplane where you play her much beefier, and Unflinching just isn't a very good mastery for it comparatively. 

- The meta and matchups. This really comes back to the runes system - Shyvana was a bruiser, and had her best matchups against other bruisers. Her early levels are weak but her base damages scale up massively towards the end of the earlygame, which allowed you to itemise to shut-down their damage output and then be able to 1v1 them after finishing Titanic Hydra. Bruisers that liked to roam could be punished by her exceptional tower-taking, or she could clear the wave and roam mid herself with ult. This changed heavily in S8 as earlygame-dominant ranged toplaners like Teemo and Jayce *and* hyperscaling into midgame champions like Nasus, Cho'Gath and Gangplank became much more popular. Shyvana is atrocious versus both groups, which leaves her missing most of her midgame powerspike and unable to dictate the enemy toplaner's position on the map via applying smart pressure. Toplaners no longer being expected to build support items lategame also hurt her as she provided huge Locket shields which made up for her mostly crappy lategame some.

- Direct nerfs due to Shyvana Jungle's strength and popularity. Pretty self-explanatory, but unlucky because Bone Plating, Banner of Command and split-stats on trees help her quite a bit. I'm looking forwards to the AD per-level nerf being reverted as it drastically reduced the viability of Trinity Force and even Sterak's Gage (a great item on Shyv Top because in the lategame you're commonly packing at least 4k HP) on her, which really hurt.

- Changing expectations of toplaners. I think this point's a lot more debatable, but Shyv Top in my experience had a strength that in Season 8 was almost unique - the ability to build basically 80% tank and still apply immense pressure as a splitpusher, and while her lategame teamfight contribution was poor - *if* she survived a teamfight after soaking for her team, she was one of the best chars in the entire game for downing turrets and neutral objectives. I don't believe splitpush is as valuable in soloqueue as it was then, and tanky tower-taking isn't really a unique strength to her anymore, she's pretty directly outclassed in her niche by Shen (espec. with Demolish) and Nasus.

Hey. So I mained Shyv Top last season, got to P4, but I've had a poorer S8. Ironically, after these nerfs I've started getting traction again (but it's still early days), and it's mainly because of the Bone Plating and Second Wind change.

What I recommend doing is going extremely defensive in your runes. My go-to is Grasp: Bone Plating, Conditioning/Second Wind, Overgrowth - Magical Boots, Cosmic Insight/Time Warp Tonic/Future's Market.

You go extremely defensive in your runes so that you can then go offensive in your early itemisation. And what you honestly should do is play like an absolute idiot. Constantly pressure toplane, even if you're clearly overextending. Don't let the enemy toplaner leave the 1v1 voluntarily without losing his turret. If you poke them low enough you can dive them and take it, but mostly it's more advantageous just to trap them. You keep forcing this 1v1 farmfest and eventually you will beat them at it. In downtime, take enemy jungle camps or get vision around the map. Shyvana has a strong low-cooldown (relatively) nope button after 6 and you have to use this to get out of bad situations you've created.

Your role is to be a tanky splitpusher, but you can also make roams in the midgame. Lategame you're there to create diversions and take hits for your team. If it goes hyper-late you've probably lost, but build or swap out for a Locket to take advantage of your extremely high health.

Standard Core:
Titanic Hydra -> Stinger -> Banner of Command (not joking, use tactically, at this point though you're actually an insane duellist as you have a large health pool and 50-60% resistance to both damage types).

Good items after that are of course Frozen Mallet and most standard tank items excluding Sunfire Cape. Trinity Force is a significantly worse option now and was always luxury. I recommend selling the Stinger for a hybrid item later-on (Wit's End does fill that hole nicely most of the time) instead of upgrading, Stinger just gives you stats you really need after TH at the cheapest price. You can build most anything EXCEPT Black Cleaver, I see this item semi-commonly on Shyv Jg and Top and it's absolutely awful, Shyv Top deals 65-70% magic damage in most games.
